planting.note: Plant container-grown or grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; SAA-Zimmerman needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: SAA-Zimmerman is a New York-origin pawpaw selected as a seedling in 1982 by pomologist John Gordon from seed collected from G.A. Zimmerman's original tree, and it is a distinct clone from the similarly named 'Zimmerman' cultivar despite the shared name. Fruit is large, averaging roughly 6 to 8 ounces, with yellow skin and yellow flesh and notably few seeds for the species, ripening in the late-season window. Plant it with an unrelated cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby for cross-pollination, since pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen. Grow it like other pawpaws in moist, humus-rich soil, starting young trees in partial shade before moving them toward full sun as they mature.
sources: Kentucky State University School of Agriculture, Communities, and the Environment — Pawpaw Program (Table 3: Pawpaw Cultivars)
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Pawpaw Variety Development: A History and Future Directions
North Carolina State Extension

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Rajada resembles 'Paulista' in vigor and habit, and young trees need frost protection below 28F while mature trees tolerate brief dips into the mid-20s.

directions: Rajada produces exceptionally large jaboticaba fruit with thinner, green-bronze skin than the related 'Paulista' selection, wrapped around sweet, richly flavored pulp. The tree's growth habit and vigor closely resemble 'Paulista', bearing a single concentrated midseason flush of trunk-borne fruit clusters rather than the near-continuous cropping of 'Sabara'. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and shelter young trees from temperatures below the upper 20s F, since cold hardiness improves only as the tree matures. Harvest fruit promptly once fully colored, as ripe jaboticaba ferments quickly left on the tree.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Jaboticaba Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jaboticaba Production in Florida
Purdue University Horticulture — Jaboticabas (Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Ponhema is a very large, extremely productive jaboticaba grown mainly for preserves; young trees need frost protection below 28F.

directions: Ponhema is a distinctive jaboticaba selection bearing large, turnip-shaped fruit with a pointed apex and a somewhat tougher, leathery skin than typical jaboticaba cultivars. Because the pulp is less palatable raw unless fully ripe, growers most often use it for jellies and preserves, where the flavor concentrates well. The tree itself is very large and extremely productive once established, making it a good choice for growers wanting volume for processing rather than only fresh eating. Grow it as you would other jaboticaba, in full sun and fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, with winter protection for young trees in marginal zone 9 plantings.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Jaboticaba Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jaboticaba Production in Florida
Purdue University Horticulture — Jaboticabas (Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Coleman is a naturally dwarf selection, so it needs less room than most white sapote cultivars but can be harder to source due to difficult propagation.

directions: Coleman is one of the earliest white sapote selections named in California, grown as a naturally dwarf, compact tree with distinctively twisted leaflets that make it easy to identify. The oblate, lobed fruit reaches about 3 inches across, with yellow-green skin and sweet, high-sugar flesh that carries a slightly resinous edge some growers find distinctive. Fruit can hang on the tree from late fall into the following summer, giving an unusually extended harvest window compared to most white sapote cultivars. Because Coleman roots and grafts less readily than other selections, source a tree from a nursery experienced with the cultivar rather than attempting to propagate it at home.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Ecke's skin color is not a reliable ripeness indicator, since it turns bright yellow well before the fruit is actually ready to pick.

directions: Ecke is a 1963 Encinitas, California selection valued for fruit that is unusually uniform in size and shape compared to the typical variability seen in white sapote seedlings. Its skin begins turning bright yellow months before the fruit is actually ready, which can mislead growers into harvesting too early, so judge ripeness by a slight give at the stem end rather than by color alone. Grow it like other white sapote cultivars, in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind, allowing ample room for a large, long-lived canopy. Thin excess fruit on young trees to encourage larger, better-formed sapotes in later years.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Michele bears nearly year-round rather than in one concentrated flush.

directions: Michele is a 1940 Pasadena, California selection grown for its small, yellowish fruit with a distinctive caramel-like flavor note that sets it apart from other white sapote cultivars. The tree bears nearly year-round rather than in one concentrated flush, making it a good choice for home growers who want a steady trickle of fruit rather than one large harvest to process at once. Culture is standard for the species: full sun, well-drained fertile soil, and shelter from strong wind while young. Because individual fruits run smaller than most named selections, plant Michele where easy snacking access matters more than maximizing fruit size.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Stickley is a seedling selection of 'Vernon' chosen for earlier ripening, so interplanting the two can help ensure good pollination.

directions: Stickley is a 1967 La Mesa, California seedling selection of the well-known 'Vernon' white sapote, chosen for ripening notably earlier in the season than its parent. Fruit is uniformly large, with yellow-green skin and sweet flesh, giving growers an early-season option to extend the white sapote harvest window when paired with later cultivars. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with wind protection, following the same culture used for other grafted white sapote selections. Because it shares parentage with Vernon, interplanting the two can help ensure reliable pollination and fruit set.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Gillespie is a notably prolific bearer once established.

directions: Gillespie is a California white sapote selection bearing round, roughly 3-inch fruit with light green skin blushed with a russet cheek on the sun-exposed side. The white flesh has very good flavor, and the tree is a notably prolific, reliable bearer once established. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind, allowing plenty of room for a large mature canopy. Thin heavy fruit sets in productive years to keep fruit size consistent and reduce the risk of limb breakage.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Harvey is known as a prolific, dependable bearer.

directions: Harvey is a California white sapote selection producing round fruit around 3.5 inches across, with smooth yellow-green skin marked by an orange-tinged cheek and cream to pale-yellow flesh. It is known as a prolific, dependable bearer, making it a solid choice where consistent production matters more than show-fruit size. Culture follows standard white sapote practice: full sun, fertile well-drained soil, wind shelter while young, and generous spacing for a large long-term canopy. Harvest when fruit yields to gentle pressure at the stem end and finish ripening indoors for the best eating quality.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Maltby, also recorded as 'Nancy Maltby', was one of the earlier white sapote selections grown commercially in California.

directions: Maltby, also recorded as 'Nancy Maltby', is a 1928 Carlsbad, California selection bred by Guy Maltby, bearing round, large fruit with smooth yellow-green skin and good flavor that carries a mild bitter edge compared to sweeter modern cultivars. It is a good, consistent bearer and was historically significant as one of the earlier named white sapote selections grown commercially. Grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil with wind protection, spacing trees well apart to accommodate a large mature canopy. Because the bitterness is more pronounced in underripe fruit, let Maltby soften fully before eating for the best flavor.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Parroquia is a fairly prolific California selection.

directions: Parroquia is a California white sapote selection with oval fruit around 2.5 by 3 inches, smooth yellow-green skin, and ivory flesh of very good flavor. The tree is a fairly prolific bearer, producing reliable crops once established in a suitably warm, frost-protected site. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with shelter from strong wind, following the same general culture as other grafted white sapote cultivars. Allow several years after planting before expecting a full crop, as is typical for the species.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (White Sapote)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Florida ripens in spring but has less cold tolerance than selections like 'Pace' or 'Copan', so reserve it for the warmest zone 10-11 sites.

directions: Florida is a tall, vigorous mamey sapote selection that ripens in spring, typically March into April, bearing heavily on a tree that lacks the cold tolerance of selections like 'Pace' or 'Copan'. Fruit size is quite variable, ranging from about 14 ounces up to a bit over 2 pounds, with pink-red flesh of good flavor. Because of its limited cold hardiness, reserve Florida for the warmest, most sheltered zone 10-11 sites and protect young trees through their first several winters. Grow it like other mamey sapote cultivars, in full sun on deep, fertile, well-drained soil, allowing ample room for a tall, long-lived canopy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Mayapan is among the more cold-tolerant named mamey sapote selections and bears a summer crop.

directions: Mayapan is a tall, upright mamey sapote selection that bears heavily in summer, typically July into August, with fruit running from about 18 ounces up to roughly 2.5 pounds and rich red pulp. It is among the more cold-tolerant named mamey sapote cultivars, making it a useful option for growers at the cooler edge of the crop's zone 10 range. Culture matches other grafted mamey sapote selections: full sun, deep fertile well-drained soil, and generous spacing for a large, long-term canopy. Expect several years after planting before the tree reaches full bearing.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Lorito bears a concentrated summer crop of smaller, easy-to-use fruit.

directions: Lorito is a Fairchild-selected mamey sapote bearing a concentrated summer crop, typically July into August, of roughly 14-ounce fruit with dark red pulp and excellent flavor. It is a smaller-fruited selection compared to giants like 'Magana', making individual fruit easier to use at the table without waste. Grow it as you would other named mamey sapote cultivars: full sun, deep fertile well-drained soil, and shelter from wind and cold while the tree is young. Allow a long runway to first fruiting, as is typical for grafted mamey sapote trees.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Piloto is slower to begin bearing and less cold-hardy than selections like 'Pace', so it suits only well-established warm sites.

directions: Piloto is a medium-sized mamey sapote tree that ripens its crop in late summer into fall, typically August through September, bearing moderate yields of 14- to 26-ounce fruit with pink-red flesh of excellent flavor. It is slower to begin bearing and less cold-hardy than selections such as 'Pace' or 'Magana', so it suits only the warmest, most established Gulf Coast or South Florida plantings. Grow it in full sun on deep, fertile, well-drained soil, with wind and frost protection for young trees. Its later fruiting season can help extend the home harvest window when grown alongside earlier selections.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Lara is a relatively cold-hardy selection bearing a late-summer-into-fall crop.

directions: Lara is a cold-hardy mamey sapote selection bearing a late-summer-into-fall crop, typically August through September, of 14-ounce to roughly 2.5-pound fruit with red pulp and excellent flavor. Its relative cold tolerance makes it a reasonable choice for growers at the margins of the mamey sapote's zone 10 range who still want strong fruit quality. Grow it in full sun on deep, fertile, well-drained soil, following the same general culture as other grafted mamey sapote selections, with wind shelter and cold protection while trees are young. Space generously to allow for a large, long-lived canopy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Chenox fruits in late spring, filling the gap between earlier and main-season selections.

directions: Chenox is a Lawrence Zill selection introduced from Belize and tested at the UF Homestead research station, fruiting in late spring, typically May into June, filling part of the gap between earlier selections like 'Magana' and the main summer crop. The medium-sized tree yields moderate crops of 14- to 30-ounce fruit with pink flesh and good flavor. Grow it like other grafted mamey sapote cultivars, in full sun on deep, fertile, well-drained soil with shelter from wind and cold while young. Its mid-season timing makes it a useful companion planting to spread the harvest across more of the year.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Viejo is cold-hardy and begins bearing earlier after planting than many other named selections.

directions: Viejo is a Guatemalan-origin, cold-hardy, early-producing mamey sapote selection with a spreading growth habit, bearing a winter crop in December when few other fresh tree fruits are available. Fruit runs 16 to 20 ounces with deep red pulp of excellent flavor, and the tree begins bearing sooner after planting than many other named selections. Its combination of cold tolerance and early bearing makes it a practical choice for growers establishing their first mamey sapote tree. Grow it in full sun on deep, fertile, well-drained soil, with wind and frost protection during the first winters after planting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Akil Especial bears compact, dark-red-fleshed fruit.

directions: Akil Especial is a Cuban-origin mamey sapote selection bearing relatively compact, roughly 13-ounce fruit with dark red pulp and good flavor. It is less widely documented for home landscape performance than older standbys like 'Pantin' or 'Pace', but it remains part of the named germplasm maintained in USDA and University of Florida mamey sapote collections. Grow it as you would other grafted mamey sapote selections: full sun, deep fertile well-drained soil, and shelter from wind and cold while young. Expect several years after planting before the tree reaches full bearing, as with other named cultivars of the species.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research & Education Center — Characteristics of Mamey Sapote Cultivars for Florida
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System — Pouteria sapota cultivar collection
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (Mamey Sapote)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Merida begins bearing about 3-4 years after grafting, and its fruit matures on the tree from early to mid-November, 6-8 weeks earlier than most other black sapote selections grown in Florida.

directions: Merida, originally distributed as 'Reinecke' after the collector who sent its seed from Merida, Yucatan in 1949, is a University of Florida selection prized for ripening 6 to 8 weeks earlier than most other black sapote cultivars grown in Florida. Fruit is oblate, averaging around 10 ounces, with smooth medium-green skin that turns dull brown at full ripeness, when the firm, golden unripe flesh softens into the sweet, chocolate-pudding-like pulp the species is known for. Because black sapote trees are usually dioecious, plant Merida, which produces only female flowers, near a seedling tree with male flowers to ensure good pollination and fruit set. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, including calcareous sites, and protect young trees from any frost, since temperatures even a couple of degrees below freezing can cause serious injury.
sources: Campbell, C.W., Popenoe, J., Malo, S.E. — 'Merida', An Early-Maturing Black Sapote Cultivar, Proceedings of the Florida State Horticultural Society 101:245-246 (1988)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Black Sapote in the Home Landscape
